name: New Caledonia
summary_text: New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while New Caledonia legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.  Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.  Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination. Yagg reported that change in July 2012; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.  Placement of detainees follows the recorded legal gender marker rather than anatomy. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice puts trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees. BuzzFeed News reported that practice on 12 January 2018. The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.  France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.

sources.title: Penal Code of 1791 and Penal Code of 1810 - decriminalisation of sodomy
sources.documents: Decriminalisation of private same-sex relations in France and by extension French colonies adopting the Code; basis for legal status in New Caledonia as French territory.
sources.detail: No URL in article text; cited as Penal Code of 1791 made no mention of same-sex relations in private, retained in Penal Code of 1810 and followed in nations and French colonies that adopted the Code

sources.title: Law No. 2013-404 opening marriage to same-sex couples - Journal Officiel
sources.documents: Legalises same-sex marriage and joint adoption in all of France including all overseas departments and territories including New Caledonia; documents marriage equality enforcement.
sources.detail: No URL in article text; cited as National Assembly vote 329-229 on 12 Feb 2013 and 23 April 2013, Constitutional Council ruling 17 May 2013 that law is constitutional, signed 18 May 2013 by President Francois Hollande, published next day in Journal Officiel; overseas section states same-sex marriage is legal in all overseas departments and territories and 2 deputies from New Caledonia voted in favor

sources.title: Discrimination protections - Law of 1985, Law of July 2012, Law of 18 November 2016 amending Penal Code article 225-1
sources.documents: Prohibits discrimination on sexual orientation (1985) and sexual identity/gender identity (2012, wording replaced with gender identity in 2016); core rights machinery for LGBTQ protection.
sources.detail: No URL in article text; cited as national legislation enacted 1985, French Parliament added sexual identity in July 2012, new law 18 November 2016 amended article 225-1 to replace sexual identity with gender identity; ILGA-Europe criticism noted

sources.title: Law No. 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 - legal gender change without surgery/sterilisation
sources.documents: Allows transgender people to legally change gender without sex reassignment surgery, forced sterilisation, psychiatrist certificates; requires court application; registry office for first name; effective 1 Jan 2017.
sources.detail: No URL in article text; cited as Senate approved 6 Nov 2015, National Assembly 24 May 2016, joint session 12 July 2016, Senate 28 Sept, Assembly 12 Oct, Constitutional Council ruled constitutional 17 Nov, signed 18 Nov 2016, published Journal Officiel next day, took effect 1 Jan 2017; MP Pascale Crozon introduced bill
